title: American Airlines Slashes 2026 Outlook as Iran Conflict Sends Fuel Costs Soaring
excerpt: The carrier beat Q2 earnings estimates on record $16.74 billion revenue, but a collapsing US-Iran ceasefire and surging jet fuel prices forced a sharp downward revision to full-year guidance, sending shares down over 4%.
body:
American Airlines posted a strong second-quarter earnings beat on Thursday, delivering record revenue and outpacing Wall Street's bottom-line estimates. But the good news was swiftly overshadowed by a grim forward outlook: the Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier slashed its full-year profit forecast and warned of a third-quarter loss, as the resurgent US-Iran conflict drives jet fuel costs sharply higher.

Shares fell more than 4% in premarket trading, extending what has been a difficult year for airline stocks caught between robust travel demand and an energy market upended by geopolitical turmoil.

Strong Quarter, Weak Forecast

For the three months ending June 30, American reported adjusted earnings of $0.15 per share on revenue of $16.74 billion — a record for any quarter. Wall Street had expected just $0.03 per share on $16.7 billion in revenue, according to FactSet. GAAP net income came in at $71 million, or $0.11 per share, down 88% from $599 million a year ago.

"American delivered year-over-year revenue growth of more than 16% in the second quarter, exceeding our initial expectations and continuing the momentum we've built across the business."

— Robert Isom, CEO, American Airlines

Revenue growth was broad-based, with premium cabin, main cabin, domestic, and international segments all rising meaningfully. Managed corporate revenue climbed 26% year over year, and AAdvantage loyalty enrollments grew more than 30%.

But those gains were nearly wiped out by fuel. American's fuel bill surged 83% year over year — an increase of more than $2.2 billion — with the airline paying an average of $4.05 per gallon in Q2. Higher fares offset roughly half the fuel headwind, the company said, but not enough to prevent a steep profit decline.

Iran War Upends Fuel Markets Again

The revised guidance reflects a fuel environment that has whipsawed airlines throughout 2026. Jet fuel hit record highs above $5 per gallon in April after the onset of the US-Iran conflict disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which had carried roughly a fifth of global oil and gas shipments. Prices briefly retreated to about $2.81 per gallon in early July following a temporary ceasefire, but the truce collapsed within weeks, and the spot price of jet fuel stood at $3.65 a gallon as of Wednesday, according to the Wall Street Journal.

American now expects full-year 2026 adjusted earnings to range from a loss of $0.65 to a profit of $0.65 per share. That is a steep cut from its prior forecast of a loss of $0.40 to a profit of $1.10. Wall Street's consensus had been $0.61 for the full year. For Q3, the airline guided for an adjusted loss of $0.10 to $0.70, against analyst expectations of a $0.26 profit.

Industry-Wide Pressure

American is not alone. Southwest Airlines cut its own annual profit forecast a day earlier, citing the same fuel headwinds. Alaska Air pulled its full-year outlook entirely after mixed Q1 results, while Delta and United have said strong demand and premium pricing should help absorb some of the blow. Across the US industry, airline fuel bills jumped 85% in May alone, totaling nearly $6.7 billion.

For travelers — including the large Indian diaspora corridor between the US and India — the cost crunch is translating into higher ticket prices. Carriers have been raising fares and baggage fees while trimming capacity to protect margins.

What to Watch

American enters Q3 with $11.3 billion in total liquidity and says it has addressed its only significant debt maturity in 2027 through recent financings. The key variable remains fuel: if geopolitical tensions ease and oil retreats, the carrier's wide guidance range leaves room for a breakeven year. If the Iran conflict escalates further — with Brent crude pushing toward $100 a barrel — the downside scenario looks increasingly likely.

American's Q3 results are expected in late October, by which time the trajectory of both fuel prices and the broader Middle East conflict should be clearer.
